[{:db/id 17592186203933 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5678787f-ddbb-5c28-abd5-08d5ea9f1942" "question-d7920e3b-ba93-57c2-9dd2-0e80e521ff6c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203673 :question/problem "Consider the following false statement.

If $2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4),$ then $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}.$ 

A counterexample for the above statement would be a pair of integers $a$ and $b$ such that 

$$
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid black]{\phantom{RRR} }\, (\textrm{mod}\:4) 
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid black]{\phantom{RRR} }\,  (\textrm{mod}\:4).
$$

Find the missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a)$ and $Q(a)$ as

- $P(a,b){:} \quad 2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)$

- $Q(a,b){:} \quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)$

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

Since this statement is false, its negation is true.

A *counterexample* is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(2a≡2b\,(\text{mod}\,4))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

A counterexample for the above statement would be a pair of integers $a$ and $b$ such that

$$
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2a \equiv 2b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4) 
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a \not\equiv b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203934 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-db63c74b-9d62-5b22-9fe0-003a0ca7d1b1" "question-d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203671 :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

For any $a \in \mathbb{Z},$ if $4 \mid a$ and $6 \mid a,$ then $24 \mid a.$" :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a),$ $Q(a),$ and $R(a)$ as

- $P(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a$

- $Q(a){:} \quad 6 \mid a$

- $R(a){:} \quad 24 \mid a$

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \:(P \land Q) \Rightarrow R.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬((P∧Q)⇒R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧Q∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(4∣a)\,∧\,(6∣a)\,∧\,(24∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that 

$$
4 \mid a
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
6 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
24 \not\mid a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=12$ suffices. 

Let's choose $a =12.$
Then, we have that 

$$
4 \mid 12
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
6 \mid 12
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
24 \not\mid 12.
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $a=12$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203935 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-02cf0cdd-dd4e-5a78-a0c4-272aec9af99d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203674 :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

For any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z},$ if $3a \equiv 3b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6),$ then $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6).$" :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a,b)$ and $Q(a,b)$ as

- $P(a,b){:} \quad 3a \equiv 3b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)$

- $Q(a,b){:} \quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)$

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(3a≡3b\,(\text{mod}\,6))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,6))\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exist integers $a$ and $b$ such that 

$$
3a \equiv 3b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6) 
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
a \not\equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\:6).
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $(a,b) =(0,2)$ suffices. 

Let's choose

$$
a = 0, \qquad
b = 2.
$$

Then, $3a=0$ and $3b=6.$ 

To check that this is a required counterexample, we proceed as follows:

Hence, we have that 

$$
\underbrace{0}_{3a} \equiv \underbrace{6}_{3b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
\underbrace{0}_{a} \not\equiv \underbrace{2}_{b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:6).
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, the pair $a=0$ and $b=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5678787f-ddbb-5c28-abd5-08d5ea9f1942" :question/id #uuid "5678787f-ddbb-5c28-abd5-08d5ea9f1942" :question/math-academy-id "q-221959" :question/problem "Consider the following false statement.

{{field-1}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a)$ and $Q(a)$ as

- $P(a):\,a<b$

our statement can be written as

$$

$$

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(a<b)\,∧\,(3a-1\ge 2b+10).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

A counterexample for the above statement would be an integer $a$ such that 

$$
a<b\,\text{and}\,3a-1\ge 2b+10.

"question-d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754" :question/id #uuid "d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754" :question/math-academy-id "q-221742" :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

For any $a\in Z,$ if $10∣a$ and $15∣a,$ then $150∣a.$

To {{field-1}} a universal statement, it's sufficient to find {{field-2}}. 
In other words, we need to show that {{field-3}}

$$
{{field-4}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-5}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-6}}.
$$

Let's choose $a=$ {{field-7}}.
Then, we have that 

$$
10{{field-8}}30\,\text{and}\,15{{field-9}}30\,\text{and}\,150{{field-10}}30.
$$

So, $a=$ {{field-11}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a),$ $Q(a),$ and $R(a)$ as

- $P(a):\,10∣a$

- $Q(a):\,15∣a$

- $R(a):\,150∣a$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬((P∧Q)⇒R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧Q∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(10∣a)\,∧\,(15∣a)\,∧\,(150∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that 

$$
10∣a\,\text{and}\,15∣a\,\text{and}\,150∤a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=30$ suffices. 

Let's choose $a=30.$
Then, we have that 

$$
10∣30\,\text{and}\,15∣30\,\text{and}\,150∤30.
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $a=30$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-605bde41-5797-5efa-814b-4ffed494727d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205223 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements. 

Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:

$$
\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)
$$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true. 

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,P∧¬Q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q,$ it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

*For any $a \in \mathbb{Z},$ if $2 \mid a,$ then $4 \mid a$*

By denoting the predicates $P$ and $Q$ as

- $P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a$

- $Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a$

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of $a$ such that its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(2∣a)\,∧\,(4∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

*To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that* 

$$
2 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=2$ suffices. 

*Let's choose $a = 2.$ Then, we have that*

$$
2 \mid 2
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid 2.
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

*So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*

Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205277 :tutorial/content "Disprove the following statement:

*For any $a \in \mathbb{Z},$ if $2 \mid a,$ then $4 \mid a.$*

Counterexample:

*To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that* 

$$
2 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid a.
$$

*Let's choose $a = 2.$ Then, we have that*

$$
2 \mid 2
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid 2.
$$

*So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204128 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

A *counterexample* is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(2a≡2b\,(\text{mod}\,4))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2a \equiv 2b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4) 
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬((P∧Q)⇒R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧Q∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(4∣a)\,∧\,(6∣a)\,∧\,(24∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample.

$$
4 \mid a
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
6 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=12$ suffices.

$$
4 \mid 12
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
6 \mid 12
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad

Finally, we state our conclusion:

our statement can be written as

Therefore, the given statement is false." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5678787f-ddbb-5c28-abd5-08d5ea9f1942" :question/id #uuid "5678787f-ddbb-5c28-abd5-08d5ea9f1942" :question/math-academy-id "q-221959" :question/problem "Consider the following false statement.

{{field-1}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-2}}.

- $P(a):\,3∣a$

- $Q(a):\,6∣a$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a\in Z,\,P⇒Q.
$$

A *counterexample* is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(3∣a)\,∧\,(6∤a).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

A counterexample for the above statement would be an integer $a$ such that 

$$
3∣a\,\text{and}\,6∤a.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-612421c3-9ef7-51ac-9c53-676106d03320" "answer-field-ad76e8a7-4f4a-5af2-bba2-21dbd8fbcccd"] :db/ensure "question-d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754" :question/id #uuid "d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754" :question/math-academy-id "q-221742" :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

For any $a\in Z,$ if $10∣a$ and $15∣a,$ then $150∣a.$

To {{field-1}} a universal statement, it's sufficient to find {{field-2}}. 
In other words, we need to show that {{field-3}}

$$
{{field-4}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-5}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-6}}.
$$

Let's choose $a=$ {{field-7}}.
Then, we have that 

$$
10{{field-8}}30\,\text{and}\,15{{field-9}}30\,\text{and}\,150{{field-10}}30.
$$

So, $a=$ {{field-11}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a),$ $Q(a),$ and $R(a)$ as

- $P(a):\,10∣a$

- $Q(a):\,15∣a$

- $R(a):\,150∣a$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬((P∧Q)⇒R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧Q∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(10∣a)\,∧\,(15∣a)\,∧\,(150∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that 

$$
10∣a\,\text{and}\,15∣a\,\text{and}\,150∤a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=30$ suffices. 

Let's choose $a=30.$

So, the pair $a=$ {{field-10}} and $b=$ {{field-11}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a,b)$ and $Q(a,b)$ as

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q.

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,8))\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

In other words, we need to show that there exist integers $a$ and $b$ such that

a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,\text{and}\,a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,8).

$$
a=0,\,b=2.

{{field-4}}(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{field-5}}(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

$$

$$

Hence, we have that 

$$
{{20}_{⏟}}_{5a}{{field-10}}{{40}_{⏟}}_{5b}\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{4}_{⏟}}_{a}{{field-11}}{{8}_{⏟}}_{b}\,(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

So, the pair $a=$ {{field-12}} and $b=$ {{field-13}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a,b)$ and $Q(a,b)$ as

- $P(a,b):\,5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20)$

- $Q(a,b):\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,20)$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,20))\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exist integers $a$ and $b$ such that 

$$
5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,20)
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $(a,b)=(4,8)$ suffices. 

Let's choose

$$
a=4,\,b=8.
$$

Then, $5a=20$ and $5b=40.$ 

To check that this is a required counterexample, we proceed as follows:

Hence, we have that 

$$
{{20}_{⏟}}_{5a}≡{{40}_{⏟}}_{5b}\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{4}_{⏟}}_{a}≢{{8}_{⏟}}_{b}\,(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, the pair $a=4$ and $b=8$ is our counterexample. \forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)
$$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true. 

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,P∧¬Q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q,$ it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of $a$ such that its negation is true.

$$

$$

So, we begin as follows:

*To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that* 

$$
2 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=2$ suffices.

$$

{{field-4}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-5}}\,\text{and}\,{{field-6}}.

So, $a=$ {{field-11}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] ["question-d1cc0610-ee4b-58b1-8b76-c910ff50a754" :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a),$ $Q(a),$ and $R(a)$ as

- $P(a):\,10∣a$

- $Q(a):\,15∣a$

- $R(a):\,150∣a$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)⇒R) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬((P∧Q)⇒R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(P∧Q)∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧Q∧¬R \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(10∣a)\,∧\,(15∣a)\,∧\,(150∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that 

$$
10∣a\,\text{and}\,15∣a\,\text{and}\,150∤a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=30$ suffices. 

Let's choose $a=30.$
Then, we have that 

$$
10∣30\,\text{and}\,15∣30\,\text{and}\,150∤30.
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $a=30$ is our counterexample. - $P(a,b):\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)$

- $Q(a,b):\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,8)$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,8))\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exist integers $a$ and $b$ such that 

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,\text{and}\,a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,8).
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $(a,b)=(0,2)$ suffices. 

Let's choose

$$
a=0,\,b=2.
$$

To check that this is a required counterexample, we proceed as follows:

Hence, we have that 

$$
0≡2\,(\text{mod}\,2)\,\text{and}\,0≢2\,(\text{mod}\,8).
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, the pair $a=0$ and $b=2$ is our counterexample. For any $a,b\in Z,$ if $5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20),$ then $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,20).$

To {{field-1}} a universal statement, it's sufficient to find {{field-2}}. 
In other words, we need to show that {{field-3}}

$$
{{field-4}}(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{field-5}}(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

Let's choose

$$
a={{field-6}},\,b={{field-7}}.
$$

Then, $5a=$ {{field-8}} and $5b=$ {{field-9}}. 

Hence, we have that 

$$
{{20}_{⏟}}_{5a}{{field-10}}{{40}_{⏟}}_{5b}\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{4}_{⏟}}_{a}{{field-11}}{{8}_{⏟}}_{b}\,(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

So, the pair $a=$ {{field-12}} and $b=$ {{field-13}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] [17592186204214 :question/worked-solution "By denoting $P(a,b)$ and $Q(a,b)$ as

- $P(a,b):\,5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20)$

- $Q(a,b):\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,20)$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a,b\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a,b\in Z,\,(5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20))\,∧\,(a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,20))\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. 
In other words, we need to show that there exist integers $a$ and $b$ such that 

$$
5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,20)
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $(a,b)=(4,8)$ suffices. 

Let's choose

$$
a=4,\,b=8.
$$

Then, $5a=20$ and $5b=40.$ 

To check that this is a required counterexample, we proceed as follows:

Hence, we have that 

$$
{{20}_{⏟}}_{5a}≡{{40}_{⏟}}_{5b}\,(\text{mod}\,20)\,\text{and}\,{{4}_{⏟}}_{a}≢{{8}_{⏟}}_{b}\,(\text{mod}\,20).
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, the pair $a=4$ and $b=8$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] [17592186204214 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186199899 :answer-field/correct 17592186199901] [17592186199892 :answer-field/correct Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:

$$
\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)
$$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true. 

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃x\in Z,\,P∧¬Q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q,$ it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example."] [17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

*For any $a \in \mathbb{Z},$ if $2 \mid a,$ then $4 \mid a$*

By denoting the predicates $P$ and $Q$ as

- $P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a$

- $Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a$

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.
$$

We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of $a$ such that its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀a\in Z,\,P⇒Q) & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(P⇒Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,¬(¬P∨Q) \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,P∧¬Q \\  & ≡\,∃a\in Z,\,(2∣a)\,∧\,(4∤a)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

*To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that* 

$$
2 \mid a  
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid a.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=2$ suffices. 

*Let's choose $a = 2.$ Then, we have that*

$$
2 \mid 2
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
4 \not\mid 2.
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

*So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*

Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument."] [17592186205277 :tutorial/content "Disprove the following statement:

> $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2a \equiv 2b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4) \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a \not\equiv b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)$."} {:db/id 17592186049004} {:db/id 17592186049805} {:db/id 17592186050369} {:db/id 17592186204216 :question/id #uuid "066de6f4-2a67-561c-8567-c6b0851ef361" :question/math-academy-id "q-185003"} {:db/id 17592186204311 :question/id #uuid "4755caee-eb84-59b9-b730-741bfb617861" :question/math-academy-id "q-221732"} {:db/id 17592186203934 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203671 :question/id #uuid "5efb9740-c4ea-5dab-b927-336adacf5d60" :question/math-academy-id "e-13340"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0394e4c4-97f7-556c-a7c1-ddf4cde28237" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048604}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204215 :question/id #uuid "379a348c-bf1b-50a7-b409-4c7b7d92ac90" :question/math-academy-id "q-184821"} {:db/id 17592186204218 :question/id #uuid "d5973acc-d30a-5e79-bac5-733767483674" :question/math-academy-id "q-185010"}] :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Divisibility Statements"} {:db/id 17592186203671 :question/id #uuid "5efb9740-c4ea-5dab-b927-336adacf5d60" :question/math-academy-id "e-13340" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186203934 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0394e4c4-97f7-556c-a7c1-ddf4cde28237" :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Divisibility Statements"}] :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

our statement can be written as
$\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \:(P \land Q) \Rightarrow R$.

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)⇒R) \mid ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬((P∧Q)⇒R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧Q∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (4∣a)∧(6∣a)∧(24∤a)
$$

> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample.

> Let's choose $a =12$.
> Then, we have that
> $4 \mid 12 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 6 \mid 12 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 24 \not\mid 12$.

Finally, we state our conclusion:

> So, $a=12$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."} {:db/id 17592186048604} {:db/id 17592186204215 :question/id #uuid "379a348c-bf1b-50a7-b409-4c7b7d92ac90" :question/math-academy-id "q-184821"} {:db/id 17592186204218 :question/id #uuid "d5973acc-d30a-5e79-bac5-733767483674" :question/math-academy-id "q-185010"} {:db/id 17592186203935 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203674 :question/id #uuid "ead69480-6713-5c2f-ad87-c2caa35de588" :question/math-academy-id "e-13356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cfa972be-3517-5432-8d4c-c787e2a63633" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050689}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204214 :question/id #uuid "ede85229-ac6b-539d-a1ef-b131f6c0e688" :question/math-academy-id "q-184797"} {:db/id 17592186204219 :question/id #uuid "fc6b2f46-431b-58e8-aa74-a0d819f58284" :question/math-academy-id "q-185014"}] :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Congruences"} {:db/id 17592186203674 :question/id #uuid "ead69480-6713-5c2f-ad87-c2caa35de588" :question/math-academy-id "e-13356" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186203935 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cfa972be-3517-5432-8d4c-c787e2a63633" :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Congruences"}] :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

"8cb314f5-21fe-5471-a157-6d01a0435299" :topic/math-academy-id 4927} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186204722 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205223 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements.

Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:
$\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀x ∈ Z, P⇒Q) \mid ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, P∧¬Q
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "30ca228b-fb65-5f29-b595-1982fc663520" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8362 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0f8e0e69-6710-5e49-82a0-5871fdb9f048" :step/math-academy-id 162530 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204723}} {:db/id 17592186204723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

> *For any $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, if $2 \mid a$, then $4 \mid a$*

By denoting the predicates $P$ and $Q$ as

- $P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a$
- $Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a$

our statement can be written as
$\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q$.

We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of $a$ such that its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀a ∈ Z, P⇒Q) \mid ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (2∣a)∧(4∤a)
$$

So, we begin as follows:

> *To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that*
> $2 \mid a \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid a$.

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=2$ suffices.

> *Let's choose $a = 2$. Then, we have that*
> $2 \mid 2 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid 2$.

Finally, we state our conclusion:

> *So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*

Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument." :tutorial/id #uuid "e09d3ca0-da11-51c7-8834-d9e55a13ac5f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9362 :tutorial/title "Disproving a Divisibility Statement"} :step/id #uuid "b4ace00c-cfe4-51a1-9841-468562e1e1f1" :step/math-academy-id 162531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204724}} {:db/id 17592186204724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205277 :tutorial/content "Disprove the following statement:

> *For any $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, if $2 \mid a$, then $4 \mid a$.*

> $2 \mid a \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid a$.
> *Let's choose $a = 2$. Then, we have that*
> $2 \mid 2 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid 2$.
> *So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "b019cf05-ce80-5440-9fde-c04187ec70b5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9360 :tutorial/title "Stating the Full Counterexample"} :step/id #uuid "Disproving Implications" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204128} {:db/id 17592186204722 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205223 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements.

Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:
$\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀x ∈ Z, P⇒Q) \mid ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, P∧¬Q
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "30ca228b-fb65-5f29-b595-1982fc663520" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8362 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0f8e0e69-6710-5e49-82a0-5871fdb9f048" :step/math-academy-id 162530 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204723}} {:db/id 17592186205223 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements.

Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:
$\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)$

To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀x ∈ Z, P⇒Q) \mid ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, P∧¬Q
$$

Therefore, to disprove the implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that $P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both true. This value of $x$ is a *counterexample* that disproves the original implication.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "30ca228b-fb65-5f29-b595-1982fc663520" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8362 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186204723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

> *For any $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, if $2 \mid a$, then $4 \mid a$*

By denoting the predicates $P$ and $Q$ as

- $P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a$
- $Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a$

our statement can be written as
$\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q$.

We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of $a$ such that its negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀a ∈ Z, P⇒Q) \mid ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (2∣a)∧(4∤a)
$$

So, we begin as follows:

> *To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $a$ such that*
> $2 \mid a \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid a$.

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $a=2$ suffices.

> *Let's choose $a = 2$. Then, we have that*
> $2 \mid 2 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 4 \not\mid 2$.

Finally, we state our conclusion:

> *So, $a=2$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.*

Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument." :tutorial/id #uuid "e09d3ca0-da11-51c7-8834-d9e55a13ac5f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9362 :tutorial/title "Disproving a Divisibility Statement"} :step/id #uuid "b4ace00c-cfe4-51a1-9841-468562e1e1f1" :step/math-academy-id 162531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204724}} {:db/id 17592186205279 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

17592186045417] [17592186046673 1005 17592186046979 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1007 "Methods of Proof" 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1008 "This course introduces students to proof-writing essentials, bridging the gap between pure problem-solving and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.
The prerequisite for Methods of Proof is single-variable calculus, which would be satisfied by completion of either Calculus II, AP Calculus BC, or Mathematical Foundations III." 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1009 "Students begin by mastering the basics of logic and logical operations, including statements, predicates, connectives, logical laws, logical equivalence, conditional and biconditional statements, quantifiers, inference, and formal and informal language. By solidifying their grasp of these logical fundamentals, students will have a secure underpinning that enables them to embark on their journey into proof-writing confidently.
A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
This challenging yet engaging course helps students with strong mathematical foundations build a solid base for further progression into advanced undergraduate courses." 17592186045417]
